title: Ordinary buildings that remain undamaged and usable after design-level earthquakes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a broadly applicable, affordable way to design ordinary buildings so that specified design-level earthquake shaking causes no damage requiring repair in either the load-bearing structure or its installed nonstructural systems. After shaking, occupants could immediately use the building, with working egress, elevators, and essential installed equipment, subject to declared external-service conditions and an established occupancy assessment. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The whole building is the unit of performance. Protecting beams, columns, and walls would be insufficient if damaged partitions, ceilings, façades, elevators, or equipment prevented occupancy. The target is also stricter than functional recovery: a building can retain or regain its function while still having damage that requires repair. The 2026 NEHRP material explicitly distinguishes functionality from absence of damage.

Concept boundary: “undamaged” here means that no structural member or installed nonstructural component reaches a predefined damage state requiring repair; it does not assert the absence of every microscopic or cosmetic change. “Design-level” must refer to a declared site-specific shaking demand, rather than earthquake magnitude alone. Ordinary-building applicability and a small, explicitly bounded construction-cost premium are part of the proposed advance. Isolation, damping, rocking, and component qualification could contribute if their combined whole-building performance met the target.

significance.text: Ordinary U.S. seismic design primarily protects life and provides limited assurance of rapid recovery. The practical gap is that a building can avoid collapse yet remain unavailable because its structure, installed systems, or equipment need repair. Modeling of modern reinforced-concrete residential buildings and reconnaissance after the 2024 Hualien earthquake both show why structural safety alone does not guarantee usable housing.

Conditional significance: if the proposed performance became reliable and affordable across ordinary construction, buildings using it would avoid the internal repair work and associated displacement caused by design-level shaking. It could substantially reduce repair demand and damage-driven demolition, preserve housing and workplaces, and reduce competition for scarce post-earthquake repair resources. The revolutionary step would be making this outcome broadly accessible across ordinary occupancies and structural systems; exceptional performance in a single specialized facility would establish much less.

Continued citywide activity would additionally depend on adoption, external utilities, road access, neighboring buildings, and occupants’ circumstances. Hualien reconnaissance documents these external impediments, including a case in which road closure postponed repairs for 25 days. Preventing damage within a building therefore removes an important cause of disruption without guaranteeing uninterrupted urban life. Loose contents, ground failure or fault rupture, and shaking beyond the declared design level remain additional boundaries.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is coordinated control of whole-building damage so that immediate usability and no repair-level damage become reliable outcomes for ordinary buildings under specified design-level shaking. In the reinforced-concrete residential archetypes studied by Cook, Liel, and Safiey, greater strength and stiffness reduced unsafe structural tagging but did not substantially improve functional recovery without additional nonstructural protection. This finding identifies a limitation of those studied designs; it is not a universal result for every structural system.

Both drift-sensitive and acceleration-sensitive components must be protected. Limiting relative movement between floors addresses one class of damage, while installed equipment and other acceleration-sensitive systems require their own protection. Structural members, connections, partitions, façades, ceilings, elevators, and equipment must work together without leaving a component whose damage disables the building. The reviewed recovery literature supports this coordinated requirement, but does not establish a design solution that meets the proposed no-repair target.

Engineering synthesis: the remaining barriers include controlling component demands across varied earthquake motions, accommodating interfaces and movement without repair, verifying the performance of a complete installed component inventory, and delivering the result within ordinary construction budgets and practices. Isolation, damping, and low-damage structural systems are possible contributors. The supplied evidence does not justify universal claims about their cost premiums, displacement penalties, or inability to qualify. A system that protects the main frame by damaging replaceable fuses would still miss this concept’s no-repair requirement.

A further barrier is demonstrating reliability beyond a favorable test. Earthquake demand and estimated recovery are uncertain, and component damage must be tied to explicit inspection and repair criteria. Repair-based component damage definitions provide a technical basis for judging the proposed outcome, but they do not themselves establish affordable whole-building performance or a universally accepted no-repair threshold.

current_state.text: Cook, Liel, and Safiey’s NIST publication record, dated July 5, 2024, describes a study of 60 reinforced-concrete building archetypes and states that estimated functional recovery for buildings designed to life-safety standards may exceed one year at design-level shaking. The manuscript assessed in the supplied review reports mean recovery times of 190–299 days at the 975-year shaking intensity, approximately the design-earthquake level at its study sites. These are probabilistic modeling results for regular reinforced-concrete residential archetypes, not measured recovery times from whole-building earthquake demonstrations.

The manuscript’s means of roughly six to ten months and the abstract’s statement that recovery may exceed one year describe different aspects of an uncertain distribution and are compatible. Neither supports the earlier assertion of a median recovery range extending beyond one year. Within the study, strengthening and stiffening alone did not ensure rapid functional recovery, and additional nonstructural design provisions were needed for high confidence of rapid recovery. The supplied review had manuscript text and tables, but lacked figure bodies and supplementary material; those unavailable portions cannot resolve additional numerical questions.

The supplied research attributes to Kristen Blowes, Carlos Molina-Hutt, and Dustin Cook a 2026 article titled “Nonstructural Design Requirements for Functional Recovery Performance.” It reports proposed recovery categories with a 25% probability of exceeding targets of zero days, three days, two months, or six months, and a finding about seismic equipment qualification. These details remain unverified: the source index contains no captured article text, and the supplied review could not confirm the article identity, displayed DOI, numerical targets, or equipment-qualification conclusion. This access gap does not establish that the reported findings are false.

The supplied October 30, 2026 description of the 2026 NEHRP Recommended Seismic Provisions documents new functional-recovery guidance. The reviewed Volume I material identifies an optional framework building on ASCE/SEI 7-22; it does not establish universally adopted code requirements. The available extraction ended on PDF page 49, before Appendix A’s substantive requirements, and both indexed volumes have truncated extractions. The reviewed material therefore supports the introduction of guidance, but does not verify its precise recovery-time targets or exceedance probabilities. Its distinction between functionality and absence of damage also makes clear why functional recovery is less demanding than this concept’s no-repair outcome.

Reconnaissance of 16 buildings after the 2024 Hualien, Taiwan earthquake found that nonstructural failures made some structurally intact residential buildings uninhabitable. Documented problems included egress and elevators, ceilings, partitions, façades, and glazing. The sample also included structural damage, external access and utility impediments, and buildings that continued functioning; many sampled buildings were older. It consequently demonstrates mechanisms of lost function without establishing their prevalence in modern ordinary buildings. Publication metadata differ between the landing page and PDF, including dates and author lists; the matching title, DOI, and substantive content establish article identity, while the PDF identifies June 2026 publication rather than the January 6 date reported in the earlier research.

Taken together, the supplied evidence establishes a substantial recovery problem and a move toward explicit functional-recovery design. It does not demonstrate the proposed affordable, ordinary-building no-repair capability. Nor does it establish that no qualifying example exists anywhere: the supplied review has no bounded search record supporting a comprehensive state-of-practice conclusion as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: test several fully fitted multi-story buildings representing ordinary occupancies and more than one structural system. Before testing, declare the site-specific design-level demand and a suite of appropriate earthquake motions. Shake-table tests could provide controlled evidence; adequately instrumented real earthquakes could also contribute if the measured building demands met the declared conditions. A single favorable motion or specialized hospital would not establish broad ordinary-building applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Design-level testing covers ordinary multi-story buildings across multiple structural systems

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance threshold: no structural member or installed nonstructural component may reach a predeclared damage state requiring repair. Egress and elevators must remain usable, relevant installed equipment must operate, and immediate occupancy must be permitted through an established assessment procedure. Publish the component inventory, damage definitions, instrumentation, inspection methods, and operational checks, including how concealed damage is assessed. Isolation or rocking may qualify if the complete building passes; sacrificial components requiring repair and recovery taking days or months would not.
completion_criteria.label: No repair-requiring damage, with operational systems and immediate occupancy

completion_criteria.text: Proposed affordability and boundary requirements: compare upfront construction cost with a matched life-safety-code building of the same use, using a predeclared small cost factor and transparent accounting boundaries. State assumptions about external utilities, backup services, contents, access, ground failure, neighboring hazards, and shaking above the tested level. Where immediate use depends on a service outside the tested building, report that dependency explicitly.
completion_criteria.label: Cost comparison reports predeclared small cost factor and service dependencies

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: disclose designs, component specifications, motions, measured responses, damage inspections, costs, and occupancy decisions sufficiently for independent evaluation and replication. Declare the intended reliability across motions and buildings, report failures as well as successes, and seek independent demonstrations across different structural systems and construction teams. These are proposed benchmarks, not established standards. Finite tests can demonstrate breadth within stated conditions; they cannot establish literal universality across all ordinary buildings and earthquakes.
completion_criteria.label: Replication-ready disclosures report intended reliability, failures, and applicability limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: STR-04, “Field-scale broadband seismic cloaking,” concerns modifying the seismic waves reaching a protected region. STR-10 concerns a building’s whole-system performance under specified shaking. STR-05, “Primary members whose mechanical state can be reprogrammed in service,” could provide a way to adjust structural response, but reprogrammable members alone would not establish protection of every installed nonstructural system. These distinctions use the supplied roster titles; detailed evidence for STR-04 and STR-05 was not supplied.

Roster-based overlap: STR-11, “Passive damping that removes resonant amplification from governing modes,” could help reduce building demands, while STR-01, “Flaw-tolerant bulk members at near-theoretical specific strength,” could improve member capacity. Neither title entails no-repair performance for a complete fitted building. STR-02, “Repeated autonomous restoration of full structural capacity,” addresses restoration after damage, whereas STR-10 requires avoiding repair-level damage and preserving immediate usability.

Roster-based distinction: STR-07, “Topological control that denies an undesigned collapse mechanism,” and STR-12, “Disproportionate collapse made unavailable after loss of any one primary member,” address collapse pathways and robustness. Their objectives overlap with earthquake safety but do not by themselves guarantee undamaged components or immediate occupancy. STR-09, “A prospectively validated law of structural lifespan,” concerns prediction over time; it could inform durability assessment without establishing whole-building performance during a design-level earthquake.

Roster-based relationship: STR-03, “A cast mineral solid that can be a complete primary structure,” STR-06, “Load-bearing structures that grow and remodel,” and STR-08, “Primary structure that stores the host system’s useful energy,” concern structural materials, adaptation, or combined functions. They could coexist with STR-10, but their supplied titles do not establish seismic damage prevention or immediate usability. STR-10 remains a distinct whole-building performance target that could potentially use several underlying technologies.

change_log.change: Preserved STR-10’s identity and whole-building ambition while defining “undamaged” through repair-level damage and distinguishing it from functional recovery.
change_log.reason: The reviewed NEHRP material explicitly allows functionality to coexist with damage; the proposed innovation requires a stricter outcome.

change_log.change: Replaced the unsupported median recovery range with modeled means of 190–299 days at the approximately design-level 975-year intensity, alongside the abstract’s separate possible outcome beyond one year.
change_log.reason: Means, medians, and possible long-duration outcomes are different statistical claims; the supplied review supports the means and possible outcome.

change_log.change: Limited the strength-and-stiffness finding to the studied reinforced-concrete residential archetypes and integrated the need to address drift-sensitive and acceleration-sensitive components.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports a specific modeling result and coordinated component protection, rather than a universal conclusion about every building system.

change_log.change: Removed blanket cost and displacement assertions about isolation and rocking, and made eligibility depend on whole-building performance.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish universal technology limitations. Isolation or rocking could qualify, while repair-requiring sacrificial parts would fail the proposed criterion.

change_log.change: Retained the reported Blowes article targets and equipment-qualification finding only as explicitly unverified attributions.
change_log.reason: No article artifact was captured, so the quantitative details and bibliographic identity cannot be confirmed; missing evidence does not prove them false.

change_log.change: Described the 2026 NEHRP framework as optional guidance building on ASCE/SEI 7-22 and preserved the extraction boundary.
change_log.reason: The review supports introduction of guidance, but not universal adoption or numerical requirements beyond the truncated text.

change_log.change: Expanded the Hualien account to include its 16-building scope, older buildings, continued-function examples, structural damage, and external impediments.
change_log.reason: The reconnaissance supports particular loss-of-function mechanisms without establishing their prevalence in modern ordinary construction or unconditional citywide benefits.

change_log.change: Qualified the Hualien publication date and retained the landing-page/PDF metadata discrepancy.
change_log.reason: The reviewed PDF identifies June 2026 publication, while the earlier research reported January 6; article identity is supported despite metadata differences.

change_log.change: Made construction cost, hazard demands, component inventory, inspection, service assumptions, occupancy decisions, reliability, and independent replication explicit in the proposed completion criteria.
change_log.reason: These declarations make the proposed outcome assessable while avoiding invented numerical standards or claims of universality.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical state-of-practice conclusion with a bounded assessment and explained relationships across the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence establishes the recovery gap but lacks comprehensive search coverage; related concepts describe distinct mechanisms or objectives and should remain separate.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any existing ordinary-building system already meets all proposed no-repair, immediate-use, affordability, and reliability conditions.

The Blowes article’s identity, displayed DOI, four recovery-time targets, 25% exceedance probability, and equipment-qualification conclusion remain unverified because no inspectable article text was supplied.

The substantive requirements of the 2026 NEHRP functional-recovery appendix, including precise numerical targets, lie beyond the reviewed extraction. Adoption by jurisdictions is also not established.
The Hualien landing page and PDF differ in publication metadata and author lists; the exact bibliographic reconciliation remains unresolved despite confirmed article identity.

The acceptable construction-cost factor, required reliability, motion suite, building sample, repair thresholds, and immediate-occupancy procedure remain proposal parameters requiring explicit selection.
The boundary between permitted cosmetic change and repair-level damage requires an operational definition for each component class.
The detailed mechanisms and evidence for related roster concepts were not supplied; their relationships here are conceptual interpretations of the provided titles.

brief.title: Everyday buildings usable without repairs after earthquakes
possible: People could keep using their homes and workplaces immediately after the earthquake shaking those buildings were designed for. Affordable designs for ordinary buildings would keep the structure, ceilings, walls, elevators and installed equipment free of damage requiring repair, with safe exits and an assessment permitting occupancy.
why: A building can survive an earthquake yet leave its residents without usable housing. Preventing damage throughout the building would spare households and businesses displacement and repair work, reduce demolition driven by damage, and ease demand for scarce repair crews.

sources.who: Dustin T. Cook, Abbie B. Liel and Amir Safiey
sources.showed: Models of 60 concrete building designs found that stronger, stiffer structures alone did not ensure rapid recovery. Protection for components such as ceilings and equipment was also needed.
sources.quote:
Additionally, while increased19
strength and stiffness requirements significantly reduce the likelihood of a building being marked20
as unsafe due to structural damage, additional design provisions for nonstructural components are21
required to ensure a high confidence of rapid recovery.
sources.cited_for: Protecting the structure alone does not ensure that a building can quickly return to use.
sources.not_established: The study modeled recovery; it did not demonstrate a complete building that remained usable without repairs.

sources.who: Kristen Blowes, Carlos Molina-Hutt and Dustin Cook
sources.showed: The article concerns design requirements for building components outside the load-bearing structure to support recovery after earthquakes.
sources.cited_for: The work addresses design requirements for restoring building use after earthquakes.
sources.not_established: Recovery requirements do not establish that an affordable, complete building can avoid all repair-requiring damage.

sources.who: National Institute of Building Sciences Building Seismic Safety Council
sources.showed: The council developed optional guidance for functional recovery, meaning maintaining or restoring a building's basic use after an earthquake.
sources.cited_for: Design guidance is beginning to address building use after earthquakes alongside life safety.
sources.not_established: Returning to use can still involve damage requiring repair, so recovery guidance does not establish the proposed outcome.

sources.who: Alice Chang-Richards, Ke Jiang and collaborators
sources.showed: A survey of 16 buildings in Hualien found that damaged components outside the main structure could prevent residential use. Restricted access also disrupted businesses.
sources.quote:
Business disruptions were mainly caused by restricted access or cordons put in place for the safe 
demolition of adjacent buildings.
sources.cited_for: Damage to exits, elevators and other installed components can disable buildings whose structures remain intact.
sources.not_established: This small sample, including many older buildings, does not establish how often modern ordinary buildings lose use.

shown: Cook, Liel and Safiey's modeling explains why strengthening a building alone can leave long delays before people return. Chang-Richards and colleagues observed the practical problem in Hualien: some structurally intact homes became uninhabitable because other building components failed.

The Building Seismic Safety Council has introduced guidance for recovery after earthquakes. Affordable ordinary buildings that remain immediately usable without repair have yet to be demonstrated across different building types.
missing: A complete building must protect both its load-bearing structure and every installed component from damage requiring repair.
The same protection must work across varied earthquake motions and ordinary building types.
Whole-building performance must come with a small, explicitly bounded increase in construction cost.

milestones.label: Ordinary buildings withstand their declared earthquake shaking
milestones.explanation: Several fully fitted multi-story buildings with different load-bearing systems would have to undergo varied motions matching a declared site-specific shaking level. This would test applicability across ordinary construction.

milestones.label: Buildings remain usable without repairs
milestones.explanation: Inspections would have to find no damage requiring repair, while exits, elevators and equipment work and an established assessment permits immediate occupancy. This would establish performance throughout the building.

milestones.label: Costs stay within a small declared premium
milestones.explanation: Construction costs would have to meet a small premium set beforehand against a comparable code-compliant building, with external service dependencies stated. This would establish affordability and conditions for immediate use.

milestones.label: Independent teams can repeat and assess the results
milestones.explanation: Disclosures would have to support independent evaluation and replication, state intended reliability and limits, and include failures. This would let others judge whether success extends beyond favorable demonstrations.

uncertain: The acceptable cost premium, required reliability and breadth of testing remain to be set.
Each component needs a clear boundary between permitted cosmetic change and damage requiring repair.
Immediate use may still depend on utilities, road access and hazards from neighboring buildings.

page.title: Damage avoidance design for buildings
page.definition: Residential and office buildings remain immediately usable after the site-specific design earthquake specified by their governing code, with no damage requiring repair to the structure or installed nonstructural systems, such as partitions, façades, lifts and equipment. Use is conditional on declared external services and access.

goal.need: A 2024 study modeled 60 reinforced-concrete building archetypes and found that functional recovery could exceed one year after design-level earthquakes for life-safety designs. Reconnaissance of 16 buildings after the 2024 Hualien earthquake found that nonstructural damage caused closure or restricted use of some residential buildings. Avoiding collapse therefore does not establish continued occupancy or function.

statements.quote: RECOMMENDATION 2: Design New Buildings to Meet Recovery-Based Objectives
statements.context: Recommendation 2 of their report to Congress concerns recovery objectives beyond occupant safety.

statements.body: Natural Hazards Commission Toka Tū Ake, Structural Engineering Society New Zealand and Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
statements.quote: deliver buildings that are less likely to be damaged and thereby limit disruption and losses in future earthquakes.
statements.context: The executive summary identifies this as the key goal of Low Damage Seismic Design.

completion.title: A fully fitted building remains usable without repair after its code design-earthquake shaking.
completion.criterion: A full-scale, fully fitted residential or office building undergoes shaking meeting its declared, site-specific code design-earthquake demand. Independent assessment finds no damage requiring repair in any structural member or installed nonstructural component; egress, lifts and installed systems required for the declared use operate immediately, and the competent authority permits occupancy. Component repair criteria and external-service and access conditions are fixed before assessment. This establishes performance only for the building and shaking assessed.
completion.set_by: Atlas; no external test combining the draft's requirements was identified.
completion.basis: FEMA/NIST recovery recommendations, New Zealand LDSD guidance, the 2026 NEHRP appendix, REDi and FEMA 356 were searched for a whole-building no-repair test covering ordinary buildings and a construction-cost ceiling. None was found. The narrow test retains immediate use without repairs; affordability, population reliability and applicability across construction types have no assigned threshold.

milestones.title: Mechanical and electrical equipment remains operable after its certified earthquake shaking.
milestones.criterion: Equipment passes HCAI-approved shake-table qualification, maintaining structural integrity and functionality at its certified demand and mounting configuration. A product line normally requires two representative units; one test is permitted for a single product manufactured under ISO 9001. OSP-0553, approved on 5 August 2025, includes one 75 kW gas generator, UUT-30, retaining integrity and function after AC156 testing at a short-period design spectral acceleration of 2.00 g and a mounting-height-to-building-height ratio of 1.
milestones.set_by: California Department of Health Care Access and Information, PIN 55, revised 23 October 2025; requirements concern designated equipment in facilities under OSHPD jurisdiction.
milestones.threshold_quote: Minimum of two equipment/components shall be tested for a product line with similar structural configuration.

milestones.title: A building's structure remains safe to occupy and essentially retains its design strength and stiffness.
milestones.criterion: The structure meets FEMA 356 Immediate Occupancy Structural Performance Level S-1 at the project's specified shaking demand, including applicable component acceptance criteria. Limited structural damage and minor repairs are permitted; installed services are outside this structural test. In the 60 reinforced-concrete archetypes modeled by Cook and colleagues, increased strength and stiffness reduced unsafe structural tagging, but rapid whole-building recovery also required nonstructural provisions.
milestones.set_by: American Society of Civil Engineers for FEMA, FEMA 356, Section 1.5.1.1, November 2000; this rehabilitation performance state does not prescribe one universal shaking demand.
milestones.threshold_quote: essentially retains the pre-earthquake design strength and stiffness of the structure

milestones.title: Buildings meet REDi Platinum targets for immediate reoccupancy, recovery under 72 hours and loss under 2.5%.
milestones.criterion: A building satisfies REDi Platinum's full criteria: immediate reoccupancy, functional recovery in less than 72 hours and Scenario Expected Loss below 2.5% of Total Building Value at its site-specific 10%-in-50-years shaking hazard. Downtime targets use 50% probability of non-exceedance. Total Building Value uses replacement hard costs and damageable contents; utility interruptions require backup arrangements. These are assessed design objectives that permit repair costs.
milestones.set_by: Arup, REDi Rating System, Version 1.0, October 2013; the combined numerical objectives appear in the graphic on printed page 11, with hazard and probability definitions on pages 12–17.

milestones.title: A building meets the NEHRP zero-hour recovery target with no more than 25% conditional exceedance.
milestones.criterion: An explicit assessment meets Functional Recovery Category A: a zero-hour functional-recovery target, with conditional probability of exceeding it no greater than 25% at the functional recovery earthquake spectrum, FREᵣ. The spectrum targets a 10% probability of exceeding the recovery time in 50 years. Recovery covers basic intended function and excludes external factors. This optional framework permits damage; FREᵣ differs from the code design earthquake. The 2026 nonstructural study addresses Categories B–D and excludes Category A.
milestones.set_by: Building Seismic Safety Council, 2026 NEHRP Recommended Seismic Provisions, Appendix A, Section A.1.7 and Table A.1-3; the zero-hour value is specified in the table. Appendix A is optional unless adopted.
milestones.threshold_quote: The target reliability shall not exceed a 25% probability of exceeding the target functional recovery time

not_found: No external criterion combining immediate whole-building use, absence of repairs, ordinary-building applicability and a construction-cost ceiling was identified.
No published demonstration meeting the completion test for every installed component of a fully fitted residential or office building was identified.
No qualifying REDi Platinum assessment or NEHRP Category A result was established from the opened sources.
The full text of the 2024 ten-storey TallWood shake-table paper could not be opened through ASCE or NSF.
The accessible 2026 NEHRP Volume I extraction ends during Appendix A definitions, before its detailed design and assessment procedures.

results.finding: Across 60 modeled concrete archetypes, red tags began to occur above 1% simulated drift.
results.detail: The analysis relates structural drift to unsafe tagging, but does not assess FEMA 356 S-1 component acceptance criteria or establish retention of design strength and stiffness.
results.quote: red tags start to occur above 1 % drift demand

results.finding: Ten reference archetypes averaged 151 days of functional recovery at the 475-year shaking intensity.
results.detail: The modeled recovery result bears on the recovery-time target, but the study does not assess the full REDi Platinum criteria, including immediate reoccupancy and Scenario Expected Loss.
results.quote: (average of 151 days) for a 475-year ground motion intensity

results.finding: One retrofitted residential building, S03, sustained minor structural cracking after shaking with a recorded PGA of 0.4g.
results.detail: The building received no placard, but the paper does not assess FEMA 356 S-1 component acceptance criteria at the project's specified demand.
results.quote:
The PGA experienced at the building’s location was recorded 
as 0.4g. The reconnaissance records indicate that Building S03 
performed satisfactorily and received no placard.

results.finding: For one residential building, S03, the predicted mean scenario expected loss was 6%.
results.detail: The predicted loss exceeds 2.5%, and predicted reoccupancy took 29 days. The analysis used the observed earthquake scenario, not a full REDi Platinum assessment at the specified hazard.
results.quote:
The outputs of the seismic risk and recovery assessment of the 
building using the FEMA P -58 [3] and ATC -138 [9,25] 
frameworks, the SP3 software [32], and the 2024 Mw 7.4 
Hualien Earthquake scenario showed a predicted mean SEL of 
6%.

results.finding: Tyco 4010ES fire alarm controls: 2 representative units are listed under certification up to 2.5 g.
results.detail: HCAI approved OSP-0004 with AC156 identified as the certification method and a rigid wall-mounted configuration. The supplied text does not explicitly report the units’ structural integrity or functionality after testing.

results.finding: Two Johnson Thermal Systems chillers retained integrity and functionality after AC156 testing, at certified SDS values of 2.77 g and 3.0 g.
results.detail: OSHPD approved the rigid-base-mounted chiller product line at z/h = 1. The source reports OSP-0173-10, not the specified OSP-0553 certification of the 75 kW gas generator.
results.quote: Unit maintained structural integrity and functionality per manufacturer requirements after the ICC-ES AC 156 test

results.finding: Three mtu 4R0113 DS60 generator units retained integrity and function after testing at 2.00 g.
results.detail: UUT-1A, 1B and 1C passed AC-156 testing at z/h = 1 in isolated, rigid-on-tank and isolated-on-tank configurations. HCAI approved OSP-0553 on 5 August 2025.
results.quote: All units were filled with contents and maintained structural integrity and functionality after AC-156 test.

results.finding: One modeled three-story steel moment-resisting frame was optimized for Immediate Occupancy under frequent earthquake shaking.
results.detail: The abstract associates Immediate Occupancy with the frequent hazard level, rather than the design earthquake. The supplied text does not establish that applicable FEMA 356 S-1 component acceptance criteria were satisfied.
results.quote:
As a case study, the 
seismic design of a  three-story moment r esisting frame is optimized for the linear static, line ar 
dynamic, and nonlinear static analysis methods.
